questions.question: The chapter's epigraph is about not letting computers limit what we do. Who said it, and in what work?

options.text: Grace Murray Hopper, Management and the Computer of the Future (1962)
Alan Turing, Computing Machinery and Intelligence (1950)
Edsger Dijkstra, The Humble Programmer (1972)
Douglas Adams, Mostly Harmless (1992)

questions.explanation: The word the chapter is arguably about is 'sequential' — clearing our minds of old, sequential ways of thinking is exactly what partitioning demands.

questions.question: Under what conditions is replication alone insufficient, and what is the second name for partitioning?

options.text: For very large datasets, or very high query throughput; the data must be broken up into partitions, also known as sharding
For very small datasets or low throughput; the alternative is called mirroring
For read-heavy workloads; the alternative is called caching
For write-heavy workloads; the alternative is called batching

questions.explanation: Replication means having multiple copies of the same data on different nodes; partitioning means breaking it up so each node holds a subset.

questions.question: A footnote heads off a confusion about the word 'partition'. What two unrelated things does it distinguish?

options.text: Intentionally breaking a large database down into smaller ones, versus network partitions (netsplits) — a fault in the network between nodes, which is deferred to Chapter 8
Disk partitions versus database partitions
Horizontal versus vertical partitioning
Logical versus physical partitions

questions.explanation: Netsplits are a fault; sharding is a design choice. The word is badly overloaded.

questions.question: The 'Terminological confusion' sidebar maps alternative words for partition. Which pairings are right? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: shard in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud
region in HBase, and tablet in Bigtable
vnode in Cassandra and Riak, and vBucket in Couchbase
chunk in Kafka and segment in Voldemort

questions.explanation: The book sticks with 'partitioning' because it is the most established term.

questions.question: What is the normal rule about which partition a piece of data belongs to, and what caveat attaches to the metaphor for a partition?

options.text: Partitions are defined so that each piece of data — each record, row, or document — belongs to exactly one partition, making each partition a small database of its own, although the database may support operations that touch multiple partitions at the same time
Each record belongs to several partitions for redundancy; the caveat is that reads must query all of them
Each record belongs to exactly one node; the caveat is that nodes may fail
Records are assigned randomly; the caveat is that reads are slow

questions.explanation: The 'small database of its own' metaphor is what makes cross-partition operations the hard case.

questions.question: Why partition at all, and what two distinct resources get spread?

options.text: For scalability: in a shared-nothing cluster, as defined in the introduction to Part II, a large dataset can be distributed across many disks and the query load can be distributed across many processors
For availability: so that node failures do not lose data
For latency: so that data sits close to users
For durability: so that writes survive crashes

questions.explanation: Two resources, not one: storage and compute. Those other three are replication's benefits.

questions.question: What does the chapter claim about query scaling, and how does it hedge?

options.text: Queries that operate on a single partition can be executed independently, so query throughput can be scaled by adding more nodes; large, complex queries can potentially be parallelized across many nodes, although this gets significantly harder
All queries scale linearly with node count, with no hedge
Only single-partition queries can ever be parallelized
Complex queries scale better than simple ones

questions.explanation: 'Potentially' and 'significantly harder' are the hedges — the chapter picks this up under Parallel Query Execution.

questions.question: When were partitioned databases pioneered, and who rediscovered the idea?

options.text: In the 1980s by products such as Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL; the idea was rediscovered recently by NoSQL databases and Hadoop-based data warehouses
In the 1990s by Oracle and DB2; rediscovered by cloud vendors
In the 2000s by Google; rediscovered by relational databases
In the 1970s by IBM IMS; rediscovered by document databases

questions.explanation: An old idea with a modern second life.

questions.question: Some partitioned systems target transactional workloads and others analytics. What does that difference affect, and what does it not?

options.text: It affects how the system is tuned, but the fundamentals of partitioning apply to both kinds of workloads
It affects the partitioning algorithm itself, which differs entirely
It affects nothing at all
It affects the replication scheme but not the tuning

questions.explanation: Tuning differs; the fundamentals transfer.

questions.question: A colleague reads that each record belongs to exactly one partition and concludes it lives on exactly one machine. Correct them.

options.text: Partitioning is usually combined with replication so that copies of each partition are stored on multiple nodes — so even though each record belongs to exactly one partition, it may still be stored on several different nodes for fault tolerance. And a node may store more than one partition
They are correct; one partition means one machine
Each record lives on all machines
Records are moved between machines on every read

questions.explanation: Partition membership is logical; node placement is physical, and replication decouples the two.

questions.question: What does Figure 6-1 show when partitioning is combined with leader–follower replication?

options.text: Each partition's leader is assigned to one node and its followers are assigned to other nodes — and crucially, each node may be the leader for some partitions and a follower for other partitions
One node is leader for all partitions and the rest are followers
Each partition has its own dedicated node with no replication
All nodes are leaders for all partitions

questions.explanation: Mixed roles per node is what makes the picture non-trivial.

questions.question: What independence claim does the chapter make, and what does it license?

options.text: Everything discussed in Chapter 5 about replication of databases applies equally to replication of partitions, because the choice of partitioning scheme is mostly independent of the choice of replication scheme — so the chapter ignores replication from here on
Partitioning fully determines the replication scheme, so both must be chosen together
Replication must be disabled when partitioning is used
The two are entirely independent with no qualification

questions.explanation: Note the hedge — 'mostly' independent, not fully.

questions.question: State the chapter's arithmetic ideal for partitioning.

options.text: If the partitioning is fair, 10 nodes should be able to handle 10 times as much data and 10 times the read and write throughput of a single node — ignoring replication
10 nodes should handle twice the data of one node
10 nodes should handle 10 times the data but the same throughput
Throughput scales but data volume does not

questions.explanation: Linear in both dimensions, with replication bracketed out.

questions.question: Define skew and hot spot, and give the extreme case with its numbers.

options.text: Skew is when the partitioning is unfair, so some partitions have more data or queries than others — its presence makes partitioning much less effective. A hot spot is a partition with disproportionately high load. In the extreme case all the load could end up on one partition, so 9 out of 10 nodes are idle and your bottleneck is the single busy node
Skew is clock drift; a hot spot is an overheated machine
Skew is network latency variance; a hot spot is a cache miss
Skew means too many partitions; a hot spot means too few

questions.explanation: Note the chapter's care elsewhere: a hot spot is a partition with disproportionately high load, while the Summary describes hot spots as nodes with disproportionately high load.

questions.question: Random assignment would avoid hot spots. What does it get right, and what is the big disadvantage?

options.text: It would distribute the data quite evenly across the nodes, but when you're trying to read a particular item you have no way of knowing which node it is on, so you have to query all nodes in parallel
It distributes data unevenly but makes reads fast
It is optimal in every respect
It prevents range queries but allows point lookups

questions.explanation: So the chapter instead assumes a simple key-value data model in which you always access a record by its primary key — like an old-fashioned paper encyclopedia, where you look up an entry by its title and all entries are alphabetically sorted.

questions.question: Define key-range partitioning, and what lets a client route a request directly?

options.text: Assign a continuous range of keys — from some minimum to some maximum — to each partition, like the volumes of a paper encyclopedia. If you know the boundaries between the ranges and which partition is assigned to which node, you can make your request directly to the appropriate node
Assign keys by hash; you need only the hash function to route
Assign keys randomly; routing requires a lookup service
Assign keys round-robin; routing requires a counter

questions.explanation: Two pieces of knowledge: the boundaries, and the partition-to-node assignment.

questions.question: In Figure 6-2's print encyclopedia, what do volume 1 and volume 12 contain, and what design conclusion follows?

options.text: Volume 1 contains words starting with A and B, but volume 12 contains words starting with T, U, V, X, Y and Z. The ranges are not necessarily evenly spaced because the data may not be evenly distributed — simply having one volume per two letters of the alphabet would lead to some volumes being much bigger than others, so partition boundaries need to adapt to the data
Both volumes cover two letters each, proving even spacing works
Volume 1 covers A only and volume 12 covers Z only
The volumes are hash-partitioned, so contents are arbitrary

questions.explanation: Data-adaptive boundaries are the whole point of the example.

questions.question: Who picks partition boundaries, and which systems use key-range partitioning? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Boundaries might be chosen manually by an administrator, or the database can choose them automatically
Bigtable and its open source equivalent HBase
RethinkDB, and MongoDB before version 2.4
Cassandra and Riak

questions.explanation: Cassandra and Riak are hash-partitioned. MongoDB's version qualifier matters — it changed after 2.4.

questions.question: What does keeping keys sorted within each partition buy, and what is the worked example?

options.text: Range scans are easy, and you can treat the key as a concatenated index to fetch several related records in one query. The example is an application storing data from a network of sensors, where the key is the timestamp of the measurement (year-month-day-hour-minute-second), letting you easily fetch all the readings from a particular month
Point lookups become O(1), with no example given
Compression improves; the example is a log file
Writes become sequential; the example is a message queue

questions.explanation: Sorted keys within a partition is the same property SSTables rely on.

questions.question: Give the failure mode for key-range partitioning using the sensor example.

options.text: A certain access pattern can lead to hot spots: if the key is a timestamp then the partitions correspond to ranges of time — one partition per day, say. Unfortunately, because writes are appended as the measurements happen, all the writes end up going to the same partition (the one for today), so that partition can be overloaded with writes while others sit idle
Reads scatter across all partitions, making range queries slow
Partitions grow without bound and cannot be split
Timestamps cannot be used as keys at all

questions.explanation: Monotonically increasing keys are the classic key-range hot spot.

questions.question: What is the fix for the sensor hot spot, and what does it cost?

options.text: Use something other than the timestamp as the first element of the key — for example prefix each timestamp with the sensor name, so the partitioning is first by sensor name and then by time. Assuming many sensors are active at the same time the write load ends up more evenly spread. The cost: when you want to fetch the values of multiple sensors within a time range, you need to perform a separate range query for each sensor name
Switch to hash partitioning, which costs nothing
Add more partitions per day, which costs disk
Buffer writes in memory, which costs durability

questions.explanation: The compound key spreads writes and fragments the multi-sensor range query.

questions.question: The chapter describes a 32-bit hash function over strings. What is its output range and property?

options.text: It returns a seemingly random number between 0 and 2 to the 32nd minus 1, that is 0 to 4,294,967,295. Even if the input strings are very similar, their hashes are evenly distributed across that range — so a good hash function takes skewed data and makes it uniformly distributed
It returns a number between 0 and 2 to the 16th; similar inputs produce similar hashes
It returns a number between 1 and 100; distribution depends on input
It returns a cryptographic digest of 256 bits

questions.explanation: Uniformity on similar inputs is exactly what defeats key-range hot spots.

questions.question: What does the chapter require of the hash function, and which built-in hashes must you not use?

options.text: For partitioning purposes the hash function need not be cryptographically strong: Cassandra and MongoDB use MD5 and Voldemort uses the Fowler–Noll–Vo function. Many programming languages have simple hash functions built in — used for hash tables rather than partitioning — but Java's Object.hashCode() and Ruby's Object#hash may have different hash values in different processes for the same key, making them unsuitable
It must be cryptographically strong; SHA-256 is required
Any built-in hash works, including Java's Object.hashCode()
It must be reversible so keys can be recovered

questions.explanation: Cross-process instability is the disqualifying property.

questions.question: Describe hash partitioning and the two options for partition boundaries.

options.text: Assign each partition a range of hashes rather than a range of keys, and every key whose hash falls within a partition's range will be stored in that partition. The boundaries can be evenly spaced, or they can be chosen pseudorandomly — in which case the technique is sometimes known as consistent hashing
Assign each partition a range of keys; boundaries are always evenly spaced
Assign each key a random partition; boundaries do not exist
Assign each partition a fixed number of keys; boundaries are recomputed on every write

questions.explanation: Hashing converts an arbitrary key space into a bounded numeric one that boundaries can be drawn in.

questions.question: What is consistent hashing as originally defined?

options.text: As defined by Karger et al., it is a way of evenly distributing load across an internet-wide system of caches such as a content delivery network, using randomly chosen partition boundaries to avoid the need for central control or distributed consensus
A database rebalancing algorithm defined by Amazon for Dynamo
A hash function with a stable output across processes
A method for ordering keys within a partition

questions.explanation: Its purpose was decentralized cache placement, not database partitioning.

questions.question: What does the sidebar credit consistent hashing with, and what does it deny?

options.text: It notes that partitioning proportionally to nodes corresponds most closely to the original definition, but that consistent hashing actually doesn't work very well for databases and so is rarely used in practice. Some databases' documentation still refers to consistent hashing, but it is often inaccurate — so the recommendation is to avoid the term consistent hashing and just call it hash partitioning
It endorses consistent hashing as the standard database rebalancing method
It denies that consistent hashing exists
It recommends using the term consistent hashing for all hash-based schemes

questions.explanation: A widely misused term the book deliberately drops.

questions.question: What does hash partitioning cost you, and which systems make the point concrete?

options.text: The ability to do efficient range queries: keys that were once adjacent are now scattered across all the partitions, so their sort order is lost. In MongoDB, if you have enabled hash-based sharding mode, any range query has to be sent to all partitions; and range queries on the primary key are not supported at all by Riak, Couchbase or Voldemort
The ability to do point lookups; all four systems lose them
The ability to rebalance; only MongoDB is affected
Nothing — hash partitioning is strictly better

questions.explanation: Order is the price of uniformity.

questions.question: Describe Cassandra's compound-primary-key compromise, and its exact limit.

options.text: A table in Cassandra can be declared with a compound primary key consisting of several columns. Only the first part of that key is hashed to determine the partition, but the other columns are used as a concatenated index for sorting the data in Cassandra's SSTables. So a query cannot search for a range of values within the first column of a compound key, but if it specifies a fixed value for the first column it can perform an efficient range scan over the other columns
All columns are hashed, so no range scans are possible
No columns are hashed, so all range scans work
Only the last column is hashed, and the first is sorted

questions.explanation: Fixed first column plus sorted remainder is what makes the one-to-many pattern efficient.

questions.question: What is the 'elegant' data model for the concatenated-index approach?

options.text: One-to-many relationships: on a social media site one user may post many updates, so with the primary key (user_id, update_timestamp) you can efficiently retrieve all updates made by a particular user within some time interval, sorted by timestamp. Different users may be stored on different partitions, but within each user the updates are stored ordered by timestamp on a single partition
Many-to-many relationships, using a graph model
Analytics queries over all users at once
Full-text search over update bodies

questions.explanation: Partition by the 'one' side, sort by time within it.

questions.question: Hashing reduces hot spots but can't avoid them entirely. What is the extreme case, and why is hashing powerless?

options.text: In the extreme case where all reads and writes are for the same key, you still end up with all requests being routed to the same partition. This is perhaps unusual but not unheard of: on a social media site a celebrity user with millions of followers may cause a storm of activity, resulting in a large volume of writes to the same key — perhaps the user ID of the celebrity, or the ID of the action that people are commenting on. Hashing the key doesn't help, as the hash of two identical IDs is still the same
The extreme case is too many distinct keys; hashing collides them
The extreme case is an empty database; hashing has nothing to distribute
Hashing does avoid all hot spots

questions.explanation: Identical inputs hash identically — the one case uniformity cannot help.

questions.question: What is the technique for a known-hot key, and what fan-out does it produce?

options.text: Add a random number to the beginning or end of the key: just a two-digit decimal random number would split the writes to the key evenly across 100 different keys, allowing those keys to be distributed to different partitions. But reads then have to do additional work, as they have to read the data from all 100 keys and combine it
Add a timestamp suffix, producing unbounded fan-out with no read cost
Replicate the key to all nodes, producing n copies with no read cost
Move the key to a dedicated node, producing a fan-out of 1

questions.explanation: Two decimal digits gives 10 squared, or 100, distinct suffixes — so one hot key becomes 100 keys carrying about 1/100 of the write load each.

questions.question: Beyond read amplification, what does key splitting cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It requires additional bookkeeping, so it only makes sense to apply it to the small number of hot keys — for the vast majority of keys with low write throughput this would be unnecessary overhead
You need some way of keeping track of which keys are being split
It requires the hash function to be cryptographically strong
It requires disabling replication

questions.explanation: Overhead plus new state to maintain, which is why splitting can't be applied blanket-wide.

questions.question: Whose job is it to handle skewed workloads, and what forecast does the chapter make?

options.text: Today, most data systems are not able to automatically compensate for such a highly skewed workload, so it's the responsibility of the application to reduce the skew. Perhaps in future data systems will be able to detect and compensate for skewed workloads automatically, but for now you need to think through the trade-offs for your own application
Databases handle it automatically today, so the application need not care
It is the operations team's job, not the application's
Skew cannot be reduced by anyone

questions.explanation: Note the double hedge on the forecast: 'perhaps' and 'will be able'.

questions.question: Define a secondary index with the chapter's examples, and name the two approaches to partitioning one.

options.text: A secondary index usually doesn't identify a record uniquely but is rather a way of searching for occurrences of a particular value — find all actions by user 123, find all articles containing the word hogwash, find all cars whose color is red. The problem is that secondary indexes don't map neatly to partitions; the two approaches are document-based partitioning and term-based partitioning
A secondary index uniquely identifies a record; the approaches are local and remote
A secondary index is a copy of the primary index; the approaches are eager and lazy
A secondary index is a cache; the approaches are write-through and write-back

questions.explanation: The schemes discussed so far all depend on a key-value model where records are accessed only by primary key, which is what determines routing.

questions.question: How does secondary-index support vary across systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Secondary indexes are the bread and butter of relational databases, and they are common in document databases too
Many key-value stores such as HBase and Voldemort have avoided secondary indexes because of their added implementation complexity
Some, such as Riak, have started adding them
Secondary indexes are the raison d'être of search servers such as Solr and Elasticsearch

questions.explanation: Four categories, from indispensable to deliberately omitted.

questions.question: In Figure 6-4's used-car site partitioned by document ID, which partition holds document ID 742?

options.text: Partition 1 — IDs 0 to 499 are in partition 0 and IDs 500 to 999 are in partition 1, so 499 is in partition 0, and 500 and 742 are both in partition 1
Partition 0, since 742 modulo 500 is 242
Both partitions, since the index is global
Neither — 742 exceeds the ID range

questions.explanation: Users can search by color and by make — in a document database these would be fields, in a relational database they would be columns. Whenever a red car is added, the database partition automatically adds it to the list of document IDs for the index entry color:red.

questions.question: A footnote addresses readers whose database has only a key-value model. What hazards does it warn about? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Race conditions
Intermittent write failures, where some changes were saved but others weren't
Hash collisions between index keys
Index fragmentation over time

questions.explanation: You might be tempted to create a mapping from values to document IDs in application code, but you must be very careful to ensure the indexes remain consistent with the underlying data — the chapter cross-references the need for multi-object transactions.

questions.question: Describe document-partitioned indexing and precisely what a write has to touch.

options.text: Each partition is completely separate: each maintains its own secondary indexes, covering only the documents in that partition, and doesn't care what data is stored in other partitions. So whenever you need to add, remove or update a document, you only need to deal with the partition that contains the document ID that you are writing. For that reason a document-partitioned index is also known as a local index, as opposed to a global index
Each write must update the index on every partition; it is called a global index
Each write updates a central index server; it is called a remote index
Writes do not touch the index at all; it is rebuilt nightly

questions.explanation: Single-partition writes are the entire advantage of local indexes.

questions.question: Why does reading a document-partitioned index require care, and what is the hazard?

options.text: Unless you have done something special with the document IDs, there is no reason why all the cars with a particular color or make would be in the same partition — in Figure 6-4 red cars appear in both partition 0 and partition 1. So if you want to search for red cars you need to send the query to all partitions and combine all the results. This approach is known as scatter/gather, and it can make read queries on secondary indexes quite expensive: even if you query the partitions in parallel, scatter/gather is prone to tail latency amplification
Reads must be serialized across partitions, which is slow but has bounded latency
Reads can only target one partition, missing results
Reads require a distributed transaction

questions.explanation: Parallelism does not save you from tail latency amplification, which the chapter covered under percentiles in practice.

questions.question: Which systems use document-partitioned secondary indexes, and what do most vendors recommend? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud and VoltDB all use them
Most database vendors recommend that you structure your partitioning scheme so that secondary index queries can be served from a single partition
That recommendation is not always possible, especially when you're using multiple secondary indexes in a single query — such as filtering cars by color and by make at the same time
Vendors recommend always using term-partitioned indexes instead

questions.explanation: Widely used despite the scatter/gather cost.

questions.question: Why must a global index itself be partitioned?

options.text: Because you can't just store a global index covering data in all partitions on one node — it would likely become a bottleneck and defeat the purpose of partitioning. A global index must also be partitioned, but it can be partitioned differently from the primary key index
Because indexes are always larger than the data
Because a single node cannot hold an index at all
It need not be partitioned; one node suffices

questions.explanation: The freedom to partition the index differently from the primary key is what makes term partitioning useful.

questions.question: In Figure 6-5's term-partitioned index, what are the partition boundaries?

options.text: Red cars from all partitions appear under color:red in the index, but the index is partitioned so that colors starting with the letters a to r appear in partition 0 and colors starting with s to z appear in partition 1; the index on the make of car is partitioned similarly, with the boundary between f and h
Colors a to m in partition 0 and n to z in partition 1; makes a to l and m to z
The index is not partitioned, living entirely on one node
The index is partitioned by document ID, like the primary index

questions.explanation: The index is partitioned differently from the primary key index, which is exactly what makes it global.

questions.question: Explain the name 'term-partitioned' and where the word 'term' comes from.

options.text: It is term-partitioned because the term we're looking for determines the partition of the index — here a term would be color:red, for example. The name term comes from full-text indexes, a particular kind of secondary index, where the terms are all the words that occur in a document
Because the index terminates at a partition boundary; the word comes from mathematics
Because terms are contract clauses; the word comes from legal indexing
Because the partition is determined by the document, not the term

questions.explanation: Full-text search is the origin, and color:red is the generalization.

questions.question: What does partitioning the index by the term itself versus by a hash of the term buy?

options.text: By the term itself can be useful for range scans — for example on a numeric property such as the asking price of the car. Partitioning on a hash of the term gives a more even distribution of load
By the term gives even load; by hash gives range scans
Both give range scans; neither affects load
Neither is possible for a global index

questions.explanation: The same order-versus-uniformity trade-off as for primary keys, now applied to the index.

questions.question: State the read/write asymmetry of a term-partitioned index versus a document-partitioned one.

options.text: The advantage is that it can make reads more efficient: rather than doing scatter/gather over all partitions, a client only needs to make a request to the partition containing the term that it wants. The downside is that writes are slower and more complicated, because a write to a single document may now affect multiple partitions of the index — every term in the document might be on a different partition, on a different node
Reads are slower and writes are faster
Both reads and writes are faster
Both reads and writes are slower

questions.explanation: Global indexes move the cost from the read path to the write path.

questions.question: What would an always-up-to-date term-partitioned index require?

options.text: A distributed transaction across all partitions affected by a write, which is not supported in all databases — the topic of Chapter 7 and Chapter 9
Only a local transaction on the writing partition
A nightly batch rebuild
Nothing special; it comes free

questions.explanation: Which is why in practice global secondary indexes are updated asynchronously.

questions.question: How are global secondary indexes updated in practice, and what does DynamoDB promise?

options.text: Asynchronously — so if you read the index shortly after a write, the change you just made may not yet be reflected. Amazon DynamoDB states that its global secondary indexes are updated within a fraction of a second in normal circumstances, but may experience longer propagation delays in cases of faults in the infrastructure. Riak's search feature works this way too, and the Oracle data warehouse lets you choose between local and global indexing
Synchronously within a distributed transaction; DynamoDB guarantees immediate consistency
Once per day in a batch job; DynamoDB rebuilds nightly
On read, lazily; DynamoDB has no global indexes

questions.explanation: Note both halves of DynamoDB's statement — the fraction of a second is not a guarantee under faults.

questions.question: What changes over time that necessitates rebalancing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The query throughput increases, so you want to add more CPUs to handle the load
The dataset size increases, so you want to add more disks and RAM to store it
A machine fails, and other machines need to take over the failed machine's responsibilities
The schema changes, requiring re-indexing

questions.explanation: The process of moving load from one node in the cluster to another is called rebalancing.

questions.question: What are the minimum requirements rebalancing is expected to meet? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: After rebalancing, the load — data storage, read and write requests — should be shared fairly between the nodes in the cluster
While rebalancing is happening, the database should continue accepting reads and writes
No more data than necessary should be moved between nodes, to make rebalancing fast and to minimize the network and disk I/O load
Rebalancing should complete within a fixed time bound

questions.explanation: Three requirements, regardless of which partitioning scheme is used.

questions.question: The chapter rejects hash mod N. Using its example key, where does it land on 10, 11, 12 and 13 nodes?

options.text: On node 6, then 3, then 0, then 8 — the mod-10 result is the last digit. The general problem: if the number of nodes N changes, most of the keys will need to be moved from one node to another, and such frequent moves make rebalancing excessively expensive. We need an approach that doesn't move data around more than necessary
On node 6 in all four cases, since the hash is fixed
On node 0, 1, 2 and 3 respectively, in sequence
The key cannot be placed without a lookup table

questions.explanation: Changing N reshuffles almost everything, which is exactly what rebalancing must avoid.

questions.question: State the fixed-partition strategy, and what happens when an 11th node joins a 10-node, 1,000-partition cluster?

options.text: Create many more partitions than there are nodes and assign several partitions to each node — with 10 nodes and 1,000 partitions, 100 partitions are assigned to each node. When a node is added, the new node can steal a few partitions from every existing node until partitions are fairly distributed once again: 1,000 divided by 11 is about 90.9, so each existing node gives up about 9 partitions and the new node ends up with about 90, meaning about 90 partitions move in total. If a node is removed, the same happens in reverse
The number of partitions increases to 1,100 and all data is rehashed
The new node receives 100 partitions and the others keep theirs
All 1,000 partitions are redistributed from scratch

questions.explanation: Only the partition-to-node assignment changes, which bounds the data movement.

questions.question: In the fixed-partition scheme, what changes during rebalancing and what does not?

options.text: Only entire partitions are moved between nodes. The number of partitions does not change, nor does the assignment of keys to partitions — the only thing that changes is the assignment of partitions to nodes. This change is not immediate, since it takes time to transfer a large amount of data over the network, so the old assignment of partitions is used for any reads and writes that happen while the transfer is in progress
Keys are reassigned to different partitions, and partition count grows
The number of partitions changes but key assignment stays fixed
All three change simultaneously

questions.explanation: Keys never move between partitions — only partitions move between nodes.

questions.question: Your cluster has some much more powerful machines. What does the fixed-partition scheme let you do?

options.text: Account for mismatched hardware by assigning more partitions to nodes that are more powerful, so those nodes take a greater share of the load
Nothing — all nodes must have equal partition counts
Give the powerful nodes larger partitions
Disable rebalancing on the weaker nodes

questions.explanation: Partition count per node becomes a capacity weighting knob.

questions.question: Which systems use fixed partitioning, and what ceiling does it impose?

options.text: Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase and Voldemort. The number of partitions is usually fixed when the database is first set up and not changed afterward, so the number configured at the outset is the maximum number of nodes you can have — you need to choose it high enough to accommodate future growth. But each partition also has management overhead, so it's counterproductive to choose too high a number
HBase and RethinkDB, with no ceiling on node count
Cassandra and Riak, with a ceiling of 256 nodes
MongoDB and Bigtable, with no management overhead

questions.explanation: Since each partition contains a fixed fraction of the total data, the size of each partition grows proportionally to the total amount of data — so if partitions are very large, rebalancing and recovery from node failures become expensive, and if too small they incur too much overhead. Getting the number just right is difficult when the total data volume is highly variable. A fixed number of partitions is operationally simpler, which is why many such databases choose not to implement partition splitting.

questions.question: Why is a fixed partition count bad for key-range partitioning, and how do HBase and RethinkDB handle it?

options.text: With fixed boundaries, if you got the boundaries wrong you could end up with all of the data in one partition and all of the other partitions empty; reconfiguring boundaries manually would be very laborious. So these databases create partitions dynamically: when a partition grows to exceed a configured size — on HBase the default is 10 GB — it is split into two partitions so that approximately half of the data ends up on each side. Conversely, if lots of data is deleted and a partition shrinks below some threshold, it can be merged with an adjacent partition. The process is similar to what happens at the top level of a B-tree
They use hash partitioning instead, avoiding the problem
They require the administrator to preconfigure exact boundaries
They never split partitions, relying on large nodes

questions.explanation: Split on growth, merge on shrink, with a B-tree-like discipline.

questions.question: After a split, what happens to the two halves, and what is dynamic partitioning's advantage?

options.text: Each partition is assigned to one node, and each node can handle multiple partitions; after a large partition has been split, one of its two halves can be transferred to another node in order to balance the load — in HBase the transfer of partition files happens through HDFS, the underlying distributed filesystem. The advantage: the number of partitions adapts to the total data volume, so if there is only a small amount of data a small number of partitions is sufficient and overheads are small, while with huge amounts of data the size of each individual partition is limited to a configurable maximum
Both halves stay on the original node; the advantage is simplicity
Both halves move to new nodes; the advantage is even distribution
The halves are merged back; the advantage is stability

questions.explanation: Partition count tracks data volume, which is exactly what a fixed count cannot do.

questions.question: What is dynamic partitioning's caveat, and the mitigation?

options.text: An empty database starts off with a single partition, since there is no a priori information about where to draw the partition boundaries — so while the dataset is small, all writes have to be processed by a single node while the other nodes sit idle, until it hits the point at which the first partition is split. To mitigate this, HBase and MongoDB allow an initial set of partitions to be configured on an empty database, called pre-splitting. In the case of key-range partitioning, pre-splitting requires that you already know what the key distribution is going to look like
An empty database starts with many partitions; the mitigation is merging
There is no caveat; dynamic partitioning is optimal from empty
The caveat is that partitions never split; the mitigation is manual splitting

questions.explanation: Pre-splitting trades a requirement for distribution knowledge against the cold-start bottleneck.

questions.question: True or false: dynamic partitioning applies only to key range–partitioned data.

options.text: False — it is not only suitable for key range–partitioned data but can equally well be used with hash-partitioned data; MongoDB since version 2.4 supports both key-range and hash partitioning, and it splits partitions dynamically in either case
True — hash partitioning always uses a fixed number of partitions
True — only HBase and RethinkDB support it, and both are key-range
False — it applies only to hash-partitioned data

questions.explanation: Splitting is orthogonal to how boundaries are computed.

questions.question: The chapter contrasts three schemes by what is proportional to what. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: With dynamic partitioning, the number of partitions is proportional to the size of the dataset, since splitting and merging keep each partition's size between some fixed minimum and maximum
With a fixed number of partitions, the size of each partition is proportional to the size of the dataset
In both of those cases, the number of partitions is independent of the number of nodes

A third option, used by Cassandra and Ketama, makes the number of partitions proportional to the number of nodes — a fixed number of partitions per node. Here the size of each partition grows proportionally to the dataset size while the number of nodes remains unchanged, but when you increase the number of nodes the partitions become smaller again, which keeps the size of each partition fairly stable

questions.explanation: Three distinct proportionality relationships, and the third is the only one tied to node count.

questions.question: What happens when a new node joins under partitioning-proportional-to-nodes, and what are the Cassandra numbers?

options.text: The new node randomly chooses a fixed number of existing partitions to split, then takes ownership of one half of each of those split partitions while leaving the other half of each partition in place. With Cassandra's default of 256 partitions per node, a 4-node cluster has 1,024 partitions with 256 per node; after a 5th node joins there are 1,280 partitions, again 256 per node. The randomization can produce unfair splits, but when averaged over a larger number of partitions each node ends up taking a fair share of the load — and Cassandra 3.0 introduced an alternative rebalancing algorithm that avoids unfair splits
The new node takes whole partitions from existing nodes, with no splitting
All partitions are recomputed from scratch, doubling the count
The new node creates 256 empty partitions and waits for writes

questions.explanation: Randomized half-splits, made fair by averaging over many partitions.

questions.question: Why does picking partition boundaries randomly require hash-based partitioning?

options.text: Because the boundaries then can be picked from the range of numbers produced by the hash function — with raw keys there is no bounded numeric space to sample boundaries from. This approach corresponds most closely to the original definition of consistent hashing, and newer hash functions can achieve a similar effect with lower metadata overhead
Because hashing makes keys sortable
Because raw keys cannot be compared
It does not require hashing; raw keys work equally well

questions.explanation: This is where the consistent hashing sidebar's promised payoff lands.

questions.question: The automatic-versus-manual rebalancing question is a gradient. Describe both ends and the middle.

options.text: Fully automatic: the system decides when to move partitions from one node to another without any administrator interaction. Fully manual: the assignment of partitions to nodes is explicitly configured by an administrator and only changes when the administrator explicitly reconfigures it. In the middle, Couchbase, Riak and Voldemort generate a suggested partition assignment automatically but require an administrator to commit it before it takes effect
Only fully automatic and fully manual exist; there is no middle
The middle position is automatic detection with manual data movement
All systems are fully automatic

questions.explanation: A suggestion requiring commitment is the pragmatic middle.

questions.question: Why is fully automated rebalancing risky?

options.text: Because rebalancing is an expensive operation — it requires rerouting requests and moving a large amount of data from one node to another — and if it is not done carefully this process can overload the network or the nodes and harm the performance of other requests while the rebalancing is in progress. The convenience is that there is less operational work to do for normal maintenance
Because it can corrupt data during transfer
Because it requires taking the database offline
It is not risky; full automation is always preferable

questions.explanation: Rebalancing competes for the same resources as the workload.

questions.question: Walk through the cascading-failure scenario, and the conclusion.

options.text: Automation can be dangerous in combination with automatic failure detection: say one node is overloaded and temporarily slow to respond to requests. The other nodes conclude that the overloaded node is dead and automatically rebalance the cluster to move load away from it. This puts additional load on the overloaded node, other nodes and the network, making the situation worse and potentially causing a cascading failure. So it can be a good thing to have a human in the loop for rebalancing — it's slower than a fully automatic process, but it can help prevent operational surprises
A node fails, rebalancing succeeds, and the cluster recovers automatically
A network partition causes two clusters to form and diverge
A disk fills up and rebalancing frees space

questions.explanation: Automatic rebalancing plus automatic failure detection is a positive feedback loop under load.

questions.question: What is the general name for the problem of knowing which node to connect to?

options.text: Service discovery — which isn't limited to databases: any piece of software that is accessible over a network has this problem, especially if it is aiming for high availability, and many such solutions have been released as open source
Load balancing
Consensus
Rebalancing

questions.explanation: The question is not answered once and for all because as partitions are rebalanced, the assignment of partitions to nodes changes: if I want to read or write the key 'foo', which IP address and port number do I need to connect to?

questions.question: List the three routing approaches of Figure 6-7 and the problem all three share.

options.text: Allow clients to contact any node, for example via a round-robin load balancer — if that node coincidentally owns the partition it handles the request, otherwise it forwards the request to the appropriate node, receives the reply, and passes the reply along to the client. Send all requests from clients to a routing tier first, which determines the node that should handle each request and forwards it accordingly; this routing tier does not itself handle any requests, acting only as a partition-aware load balancer. Or require that clients be aware of the partitioning and the assignment of partitions to nodes, so a client can connect directly to the appropriate node without any intermediary. The shared problem: whichever component makes the routing decision — one of the nodes, the routing tier, or the client — must learn about changes in the assignment of partitions to nodes, and it is challenging to get all participants to agree. There are protocols for achieving consensus in a distributed system, but they are hard to implement correctly
DNS, load balancing and gossip; the shared problem is latency
Client-side, server-side and proxy routing; the shared problem is security
Hash, range and random routing; the shared problem is skew

questions.explanation: Agreement on the mapping is the hard part, not the forwarding.

questions.question: Describe the coordination-service solution of Figure 6-8.

options.text: Many distributed data systems rely on a separate coordination service such as ZooKeeper to keep track of cluster metadata. Each node registers itself in ZooKeeper, which maintains the authoritative mapping of partitions to nodes. Other actors — such as the routing tier or a partitioning-aware client — can subscribe to this information, and whenever a partition changes ownership or a node is added or removed, ZooKeeper notifies the routing tier so it can keep its routing information up to date
Nodes gossip the mapping among themselves with no central service
The client polls every node on every request
A DNS server holds the partition mapping

questions.explanation: All participants must agree, so all participants must read the same authoritative place.

questions.question: Which systems use the ZooKeeper-style approach? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: LinkedIn's Espresso, which uses Helix for cluster management — and Helix in turn relies on ZooKeeper
HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka, which also use ZooKeeper to track partition assignment
MongoDB, which has a similar architecture but relies on its own config server implementation and mongos daemons as the routing tier
Cassandra and Riak

questions.explanation: Cassandra and Riak take the gossip approach instead.

questions.question: Describe the gossip alternative used by Cassandra and Riak, and its trade-off.

options.text: They use a gossip protocol among the nodes to disseminate any changes in cluster state: requests can be sent to any node, and that node forwards them to the appropriate node for the requested partition — corresponding to approach 1 in Figure 6-7. This model puts more complexity in the database nodes but avoids the dependency on an external coordination service such as ZooKeeper
They use a dedicated routing tier, which reduces node complexity but adds a dependency
They require partition-aware clients, which removes all server complexity
They use DNS for routing, which is simple but slow to update

questions.explanation: Complexity moved into the nodes in exchange for one fewer moving part to operate.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about Couchbase's routing?

options.text: Couchbase does not rebalance automatically, which simplifies the design; normally it is configured with a routing tier called moxi, which learns about routing changes from the cluster nodes
Couchbase uses ZooKeeper and rebalances automatically
Couchbase uses gossip and requires partition-aware clients
Couchbase has no routing layer at all

questions.explanation: A design consequence of the earlier rebalancing choice — no automatic rebalancing means less routing churn to disseminate.

questions.question: Even with a routing tier, clients need IP addresses. What does the chapter suggest?

options.text: The IP addresses of the routing tier nodes, or of the random node contacted, are not as fast-changing as the assignment of partitions to nodes — so it is often sufficient to use DNS to find them
Clients must be configured with a static list of all node IPs
Clients must query ZooKeeper directly for IP addresses
Clients must broadcast on the local network

questions.explanation: Slow-changing information is exactly what DNS handles well.

questions.question: What level of query has the chapter considered so far, and what does it say about NoSQL datastores?

options.text: Very simple queries that read or write a single key, plus scatter/gather queries in the case of document-partitioned secondary indexes — which is about the level of access supported by most NoSQL distributed datastores
Full SQL with joins and aggregation, which all NoSQL stores support
Only single-key reads, with no scatter/gather
Only analytics queries

questions.explanation: Which is the gap that massively parallel processing databases fill.

questions.question: Expand MPP and describe what its query optimizer does.

options.text: Massively parallel processing relational database products, often used for analytics, are much more sophisticated in the types of queries they support. A typical data warehouse query contains several join, filtering, grouping and aggregation operations; the MPP query optimizer breaks this complex query into a number of execution stages and partitions, many of which can be executed in parallel on different nodes of the database cluster
Multi-partition processing; the optimizer routes each query to one node
Message passing protocol; the optimizer serializes execution
Modular parallel partitioning; the optimizer only handles joins

questions.explanation: Stages and partitions are the units of parallelism.

questions.question: Which queries particularly benefit from parallel execution, and where is the topic covered?

options.text: Queries that involve scanning over large parts of the dataset. Fast parallel execution of data warehouse queries is a specialized topic, and given the business importance of analytics it receives a lot of commercial interest; some techniques are discussed in Chapter 10
Single-key point lookups, covered in Chapter 3
Secondary index reads, covered in Chapter 5
Writes, covered in Chapter 7

questions.explanation: Large scans are where parallelism pays; point lookups do not benefit.

questions.question: State the Summary's condition for needing partitioning and its statement of the goal.

options.text: Partitioning is necessary when you have so much data that storing and processing it on a single machine is no longer feasible. The goal is to spread the data and query load evenly across multiple machines, avoiding hot spots — nodes with disproportionately high load — which requires choosing a partitioning scheme appropriate to your data, and rebalancing the partitions when nodes are added to or removed from the cluster
Partitioning is necessary whenever you have more than one machine; the goal is fault tolerance
Partitioning is necessary for read scaling; the goal is low latency
Partitioning is necessary when replication fails; the goal is durability

questions.explanation: Two things required: an appropriate scheme, and rebalancing. Note the Summary glosses hot spots as nodes with disproportionately high load, whereas the body defined them as partitions with disproportionately high load.

questions.question: Restate the Summary's account of key range partitioning.

options.text: Keys are sorted, and a partition owns all the keys from some minimum up to some maximum. Sorting has the advantage that efficient range queries are possible, but there is a risk of hot spots if the application often accesses keys that are close together in the sorted order. In this approach partitions are typically rebalanced dynamically by splitting the range into two subranges when a partition gets too big
Keys are hashed and a partition owns a range of hashes; range queries are inefficient
Keys are assigned randomly; there is no hot spot risk
Keys are sorted but partitions are fixed in number and never split

questions.explanation: Sorted keys, range queries, hot spot risk, dynamic splitting.

questions.question: Restate the Summary's account of hash partitioning, and identify the hedge.

options.text: A hash function is applied to each key, and a partition owns a range of hashes. This method destroys the ordering of keys, making range queries inefficient, but may distribute load more evenly. 'May' is the hedge — the book will not promise even distribution, because a single hot key defeats hashing entirely. When partitioning by hash it is common to create a fixed number of partitions in advance, assign several partitions to each node, and move entire partitions from one node to another when nodes are added or removed; dynamic partitioning can also be used
It preserves key order and guarantees even distribution
It destroys ordering and guarantees even distribution; 'guarantees' is the hedge
It preserves ordering and may distribute load unevenly

questions.explanation: 'May distribute load more evenly' — deliberately not a guarantee.

questions.question: What hybrid does the Summary point to?

options.text: Hybrid approaches are also possible, for example with a compound key: using one part of the key to identify the partition and another part for the sort order — which is the Cassandra compound-primary-key technique from the body section on partitioning by hash of key
Combining local and global secondary indexes
Combining fixed and dynamic partition counts
Combining replication and partitioning

questions.explanation: Partition by the hashed prefix, sort by the remainder.

questions.question: Restate both secondary-index partitioning methods with their costs. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Document-partitioned indexes (local indexes), where the secondary indexes are stored in the same partition as the primary key and value
With local indexes only a single partition needs to be updated on write, but a read of the secondary index requires a scatter/gather across all partitions

Term-partitioned indexes (global indexes), where the secondary indexes are partitioned separately using the indexed values, so an entry in the global index may include records from all partitions of the primary key
With global indexes, when a document is written several partitions of the secondary index need to be updated; however, a read can be served from a single partition

questions.explanation: Local: cheap writes, expensive reads. Global: expensive writes, cheap reads.

questions.question: Which of these claims does the chapter support? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consistent hashing actually doesn't work very well for databases, so it is rarely used in practice — the book prefers the term hash partitioning
In fixed-partition rebalancing the assignment of keys to partitions does not change; only the assignment of partitions to nodes does
A term-partitioned index can be partitioned differently from the primary key index
Hashing a key eliminates hot spots entirely

questions.explanation: Hashing can help reduce hot spots, but it can't avoid them entirely — the hash of two identical IDs is still the same.

questions.question: How does the Summary compress request routing?

options.text: As a spectrum: techniques for routing queries to the appropriate partition range from simple partition-aware load balancing to sophisticated parallel query execution engines
As a binary choice between client-side and server-side routing
As a single recommended architecture using ZooKeeper
As an unsolved problem

questions.explanation: One spectrum from load balancing to MPP query engines.

questions.question: What does the chapter's closing paragraph name as the property that makes partitioning work, and the problem it creates?

options.text: By design, every partition operates mostly independently — that's what allows a partitioned database to scale to multiple machines. But operations that need to write to several partitions can be difficult to reason about: for example, what happens if the write to one partition succeeds but another fails? That question is addressed in the following chapters
Partitions are tightly coupled, which makes cross-partition writes easy
Partitions share a global lock, which limits scalability
Partitions are replicated, which makes writes slow

questions.explanation: Independence buys scale and costs cross-partition atomicity — which is exactly what transactions are for.
